config.note: Composed: british-ds-2 for the other passes; filler-words from british-jev-2 (jev-1.13.0, thinking off).

findings.note: The action of realizing is buried in the noun realization, carried by the empty verb phrase had come to.
The noun 'decision' carries the action; the verb 'was made' does no work.
The noun 'evaluation' holds the action; the verb 'carried out' is empty.

findings.quote: After eleven years of sitting in morning traffic behind a school bus,
findings.note: Thirteen words precede the main subject 'I'.

findings.quote: By the time I reached the top of the hill that February,
findings.note: The main subject follows 13 words of introductory clause.

findings.quote: The sidewalks along Fenwick Road are cleared by city crews
findings.note: The opening names Fenwick Road, which has not appeared in this paragraph or earlier; the previous sentences were about Carver Hill, the house, the desk, municipal snow contracts and the side streets. The link to the bus routes comes only after the subject.
Doubled pair; 'plain and simple' says one thing twice.
'picturesque' appears twice in the same sentence, first before 'row of Victorian houses'.

findings.quote: Everyone's situation is different, and what works for one person will not necessarily work for another.
findings.note: Stacked qualification: two hedges making the same limit after the disclaimer.

findings.quote: the picturesque old mill that someone has turned into flats
findings.note: Repeated example: same point in the same structure as the immediately preceding example.

findings.quote: an anchor that kept me moored to my own small concerns
findings.note: Mixed figure: the car is first a cocoon and in the next clause an anchor that moors; a cocoon does not moor and an anchor is not warm or enclosing. The draft never settles which image the car is.
Empty figure: the simile supplies no mechanism or picture beyond the literal claim that walking changed how the writer sees the neighbourhood, which the following sentence already states.

The paragraph's two anchors, a particular hill and 'that February,' are not yet available; the draft supplies Carver Hill and the first winter only in the paragraph beginning 'The first winter was very hard.'
The action noun 'review' is buried in the verb 'conduct', which does little work.
The action noun 'determination' is carried by the empty verb 'makes'; the actor's act of deciding is buried in the noun.
The draft never says who decided that all changes would go through the board process. The surrounding sentences name only the board's recurring actions, not the actor behind this decision.
The draft never says who raised the concerns. The reader needs the actor to judge how much weight the objection carries.

findings.quote: Given the results of the pilot and what both teams told us in the May retrospective,
findings.note: The main subject is preceded by 16 words. The subject is 'I'.
Three consecutive sentences open with the same two words, 'The board'. The repeated subject-verb construction runs across three sentences.
"cumbersome" repeats within two sentences, first used in "Its checklist is cumbersome for a one-line fix."
Doubled pair: 'full and complete' says one thing twice.
The previous sentence was about leads recording approvals and test-run links; admission controllers are a new element, and the link to the recorded link comes only at the end of the sentence.

findings.quote: a toll booth on the highway to production
findings.note: An empty figure: the image restates the delay claim without supplying any mechanism or comparison the literal statement lacks.
Stock image standing in for an argument about process rigidity that the draft never makes. It supplies no mechanism and invites the reader to supply the harm.
Restatement: the sentence follows the pilot results already stated and adds no fact.

findings.quote: It should be noted that the board reviewed eleven changes in those two months, compared with more than three hundred in the same period last year.
findings.note: Throat-clearing: it announces the fact instead of stating it.

findings.quote: As noted above, the board would still review every high-risk change, and nothing in this proposal would change that.
findings.note: Restatement: it repeats the earlier point that the board would continue to meet for high-risk changes.

The paragraph cites 'the pilot' and 'both teams' as known quantities, but the pilot is only described later, in the paragraph beginning 'In March and April, the Payments'. The reader cannot tell which pilot or which teams are meant where the paragraph stands.

findings.quote: At a quarter past four on the ninth of March,
findings.note: The main subject, Ellen Morrow, is preceded by eleven words of introductory material.

findings.quote: In the weeks after the water went down and the loss adjuster had come round to photograph each and every room,
findings.note: The subject, Ellen, is preceded by 24 words of introductory material before the main clause begins.
'Decision' buries the verb 'decide' inside the empty verb 'made'. The main verb does no work.
The noun 'undertaking' buries the verb 'undertake', with 'has given' as an empty verb.
The noun 'assessment' buries the verb 'assess', with 'carry out' as an empty verb.

findings.quote: Flood warnings for Quay Street were not issued
findings.note: The draft never says who failed to issue the warnings. The actor is the responsible body, and the delay is the failure the text is about.
No promiser is named anywhere in the paragraph. The broken promise is a claim of responsibility, and the reader cannot tell who made it.
Repeats 'sodden' from the previous sentence within two sentences.
Doubled pair saying one thing twice. 'Each' and 'every' carry the same meaning here.
'Affected' repeats in the third sentence ('the flood affected the people of the street') after its first use in the opening sentence.

findings.quote: Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things
findings.note: Three consecutive clauses built on the same 'some lost' template.

The previous sentence is about Tom driving to Ashby for flour. This sentence opens on gluten development, an aside that the next sentence ('By the end of March she was selling') does not continue from.

findings.quote: It was obviously a shock to the whole street. The bakery is the beating heart of Quay Street, and when a heart stops, the whole body feels it. A wave of support followed that lit a fire under the council.
findings.note: Two sentences that assert and restate the flood's emotional impact without adding fact.

findings.quote: The flood affected many people on Quay Street in many different ways. Some lost stock and some lost income, and some lost things that are harder to put a price on. It is difficult to overstate how much the flood affected the people of the street, and it would be impossible to describe every way in which their lives were changed by it.
findings.note: Three sentences restating that the flood affected the street in varying ways, a point already made by the damage and Tom's skirting boards.

findings.quote: the flood was a wake-up call
findings.note: Stock image standing in for the claim about the street. The draft never says who was meant to be woken or to what.
Extends the alarm figure with a second image, a call being answered by moving flour. The draft supplies no link between the two.
Stock image standing in for an argument the draft does not make about the bakery's role on the street. The draft gives no evidence for the claim the figure is asked to carry.

findings.quote: A wave of support followed that lit a fire under the council
findings.note: Mixed figure: a wave and a fire in the same clause cannot both hold. The draft leaves unstated what the support was and what the council did.

findings.quote: The insurance payment, when it came in August
findings.note: This paragraph breaks the flood-night account into two: it sits between the paragraph beginning 'At a quarter past four on the ninth of March' and the paragraph beginning 'She rang her son Tom', which continue the same scene.
This paragraph restates the impact already asserted in the paragraph beginning 'It was obviously a shock to the whole street' and adds no new information about the flood's effect.
The noun 'observation' buries the verb 'observe', with 'made' doing the work.
'Made' carries the noun 'decision', which buries the act of deciding.
'There was' carries the noun 'expectation', burying the act of expecting in the noun.
The noun 'determination' buries the verb 'determine', carried by 'would be made'.
"decision" repeats the root of "decided" in the same sentence, so the sentence states the same act twice.

findings.quote: It is a feeling that recurs.
findings.note: The template "It is a feeling that ..." repeats in the two preceding sentences; the first occurrence is "It is a feeling that is familiar."
'Resolution' appears twice in two consecutive sentences; the first occurrence is in the opening clause of the paragraph.
The phrase 'was arrived at' is doubled across two consecutive sentences, with the first occurrence in the sentence beginning 'There was an expectation'.
The draft never says who conducted the meeting, and the chair is mentioned only later in the draft.

findings.quote: It was decided by the committee that a decision would be made regarding the proposal.
findings.note: Restatement: the sentence repeats "It was decided by the committee" and calls the determination a decision.

findings.quote: It was decided by the committee that a decision would be made
findings.note: Repeats the earlier paragraph beginning 'It was decided by the committee thxt x determination would be made' and adds nothing to it.

findings.quote: There was an expectation that a resolution
findings.note: Repeats the earlier paragraph beginning 'There was an expectation that' and adds nothing to it.

findings.quote: Some of us left the room with the feeling that nothing had been accomplished.
findings.note: Repeats the earlier paragraph beginning 'Some of us left the room' and adds nothing to it.
